q: What are process groups, sessions and daemons, and how do nohup, setsid and disown keep a job alive after logout?
p: A session has a controlling terminal; when it closes the kernel sends SIGHUP to the foreground process group. nohup ignores SIGHUP, setsid starts a process in a new session, and disown removes a shell job from its table so the shell will not signal it. A proper daemon is better run under systemd.
tip: The modern answer is systemd-run or a unit file, which gives logging, restart and resource control that nohup does not.
a: Linux groups processes into process groups, and groups into sessions. A session usually has a controlling terminal, and when that terminal hangs up, the kernel sends SIGHUP to the foreground process group, which kills most jobs. To survive logout there are a few options. nohup makes the command ignore SIGHUP and redirect output to a file. disown removes a background job from the shell's job table so the shell does not forward the signal. setsid starts the process in a brand new session with no controlling terminal, which is closest to a classic daemon. The classic daemon recipe also forks twice, changes the working directory, closes file descriptors and redirects standard streams. In practice I avoid hand-rolled daemons and use systemd, either a unit file or systemd-run for one-off jobs, because it provides logging to the journal, restart policies, dependencies and resource limits, and cleans up the whole control group when the service stops.
f: What does the double fork do?
Why is systemd-run better than nohup?

q: What is the difference between VSZ, RSS, PSS and the working set of a process, and which should you trust?
p: VSZ is the total virtual address space mapped, much of it never touched. RSS is the resident physical memory including shared pages counted for every process. PSS divides shared pages proportionally and is the fairest per-process number. Containers care about cgroup working set.
tip: Summing RSS across processes overcounts shared libraries, so use PSS or the cgroup's memory.current for capacity decisions.
a: VSZ, virtual size, counts every address range a process has mapped, including libraries, memory-mapped files and reserved but untouched heap, so it is often huge and rarely meaningful. RSS, resident set size, is the amount of that memory currently in RAM, but shared pages, like a common library loaded by fifty processes, are counted fully in each process's RSS, so adding RSS values overstates real usage. PSS, proportional set size, divides shared pages by the number of processes sharing them, so the sum of PSS across processes is accurate, and tools like smem report it. Private dirty memory shows what would be lost if the process died. For containers, the kernel enforces limits at the cgroup level, so I look at memory.current and the working set, which excludes easily reclaimable cache, since that is what the OOM killer compares to the limit.
f: Why can VSZ be larger than RAM?
What does the cgroup working set exclude?

q: What does 'too many open files' mean, and how do file descriptor limits work per process, per user and system-wide?
p: Every file, socket and pipe uses a file descriptor. The soft RLIMIT_NOFILE limits one process, ulimit or limits.conf or the systemd LimitNOFILE sets it, and fs.file-max caps the system. Raise limits for the service, not just your shell.
tip: limits.conf does not apply to systemd services. Use LimitNOFILE in the unit file or a drop-in.
a: A file descriptor is a small integer that refers to an open file, socket, pipe or device in a process. Each process has a soft limit and a hard limit, called RLIMIT_NOFILE, commonly one thousand twenty-four by default, and a busy server holding thousands of connections quickly hits it, producing too many open files errors on accept or open. The system also has a global cap, fs.file-max, and fs.nr_open caps the per-process maximum. To diagnose, I compare the count of entries in the process's fd directory with the limits file in proc, and use lsof to see what is open, which often reveals a descriptor leak such as unclosed sockets. To fix, I raise the limit for the service. For a systemd service that means LimitNOFILE in the unit or a drop-in, because etc security limits.conf applies only to PAM login sessions. Then I restart the service and verify the new limit in its proc limits file.
f: Why doesn't limits.conf affect a service?
How do you find a descriptor leak?

q: What is overlayfs, and how does it relate to container image layers and the writable layer?
p: overlayfs merges a read-only lowerdir stack with a writable upperdir into one view. Container runtimes stack image layers as lowerdirs and give each container an upperdir. Writes use copy-up, so a modified file is copied into the upper layer first.
tip: Heavy writes to the container layer are slow and vanish with the container. Put them on a volume.
a: Overlayfs is a union filesystem in the Linux kernel. It presents a single merged directory built from one or more read-only lower directories plus one writable upper directory and a work directory. Container runtimes use it to implement image layers: each image layer becomes a lower directory, all shared between containers that use the same image, and each running container gets its own upper directory for changes. Reading a file finds it in the topmost layer that has it. Writing to a file that exists only in a lower layer triggers a copy-up, where the whole file is copied into the upper layer and then modified, and deleting a lower file creates a special whiteout marker. That explains why the container layer disappears when the container is removed, why editing large files in a container is slow, and why databases and logs belong on mounted volumes, not on the overlay.
f: What is a whiteout file?
Why is copy-up expensive for large files?

q: What do chattr and lsattr do, and when would an immutable flag explain a mysterious 'Operation not permitted' for root?
p: Extended file attributes such as immutable (+i) and append-only (+a) are enforced by the kernel regardless of ownership or permission bits. Even root cannot modify or delete a file with +i until the flag is removed.
tip: If rm fails as root, run lsattr before anything else. It is a classic puzzle in interviews.
a: Besides the normal permission bits, ext4 and XFS support file attributes managed with chattr and shown with lsattr. The immutable attribute prevents any change, including delete, rename, link creation and write, even by root, until the attribute is removed. The append-only attribute allows adding data to the end of a file but not rewriting it, which is useful for protecting logs. I may meet them when a configuration file keeps reverting, or a deletion fails with operation not permitted despite root privileges and correct ownership, in which case lsattr reveals the flag. Attackers sometimes use immutable flags to protect their persistence files, and administrators use them to guard critical files, like making resolv.conf unchangeable by network managers, though this is better handled through proper configuration. Also check mount options like read-only and noexec, and security modules, when permissions seem fine but access fails.
f: Why would an attacker set the immutable flag?
What else can cause permission denied for root?

q: What are inotify limits, and what error appears when a tool such as a file watcher or Kubernetes runs out of watches?
p: inotify lets programs watch files for changes. Limits on watches and instances per user, fs.inotify.max_user_watches and max_user_instances, can be hit by IDEs, log shippers and kubelet-heavy nodes, giving 'no space left on device' or 'too many open files' for inotify.
cmds: find /proc/*/fd -lname 'anon_inode:inotify' 2>/dev/null | cut -d/ -f3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head
tip: The misleading part is the message. ENOSPC from inotify has nothing to do with disk space.
a: The inotify API lets a program subscribe to filesystem events instead of polling. The kernel limits how many instances and watches each user can create, because each watch uses unswappable kernel memory. Tools that monitor large directory trees, such as IDEs, webpack dev servers, log agents, and nodes running many containers each with config watchers, can exhaust the limits. The symptom is confusing: errors like no space left on device or too many open files, although the disk and descriptors are fine, or a failure to start a pod's sidecar. I check the sysctls for max user watches and max user instances, and use the proc filesystem to see which processes hold the most inotify instances. The fix is to raise the limits persistently in a sysctl configuration file, for example to half a million watches, after considering memory usage, and to exclude huge directories such as node_modules or build outputs from watchers.
f: Why is the error message misleading?
How do you find the heaviest inotify user?

q: How do you use ss to troubleshoot sockets, listen queues and connection states?
p: ss reads socket information directly from the kernel and is faster than netstat. Use -tlnp for listeners, -tan for connection states, -s for summary, and -ti for per-connection TCP internals such as retransmits and congestion window. Recv-Q and Send-Q on listeners show accept backlog.
tip: For a LISTEN socket, Recv-Q is the current accept queue length and Send-Q is its maximum. A full queue means the app cannot accept fast enough.
a: I use ss for almost all socket work. With tlnp, I list listening TCP sockets with numeric ports and the owning process, which answers whether the service is listening and on which address. Binding to localhost instead of all interfaces is a classic cause of unreachable services. For a LISTEN socket the Recv-Q column shows how many fully established connections are waiting to be accepted, and Send-Q shows the configured backlog, so if the queue is at its limit, the application is too slow to accept, or the backlog is too small. With ss minus s I get totals by state, which reveal thousands of TIME_WAIT or CLOSE_WAIT sockets. A growing CLOSE_WAIT count usually indicates an application not closing connections. With the info option, I see retransmissions, round-trip time and congestion window for each connection, which helps distinguish network problems from application problems.
f: What does a growing CLOSE_WAIT count mean?
How do you check the accept backlog?

q: How does conntrack work, and when does the connection tracking table cause problems?
p: conntrack records the state of every flow so NAT and stateful firewalling work. Entries live in a fixed-size table. When it fills, new connections are dropped; stale or short-lived flows and high UDP volume are common causes.
tip: The classic log line is 'nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet'.
a: The kernel's connection tracking subsystem follows each flow through netfilter, storing source, destination, ports, protocol and state. Stateful rules such as accept established connections, and NAT, both depend on it. The table has a maximum size, and every tracked flow consumes an entry for the duration of its timeout, which is long for established TCP, around five days by default, shorter for others. Problems appear when there are very many short connections, such as DNS over UDP, or when a service handles huge numbers of clients through NAT, because entries pile up and the table fills. Then new packets are dropped and the kernel logs table full. Diagnostics are comparing the count to the maximum, and statistics showing insert failures or drops. Fixes include increasing nf_conntrack_max and the hash size, reducing timeouts, bypassing tracking for traffic that does not need it with the raw table's NOTRACK, and reusing connections.
f: How do you bypass conntrack?
Why is the TCP established timeout so long?

q: How do you troubleshoot DNS from a Linux host using dig, resolvectl and nsswitch, and why can dig work while an application fails?
p: dig talks directly to a DNS server and ignores nsswitch, /etc/hosts and local caches. Applications use the libc resolver which follows nsswitch.conf order, search domains and ndots. Compare dig with getent hosts to see what the application sees.
tip: getent hosts uses the same path as most applications, so it is the right tool to reproduce their behaviour.
a: dig is a pure DNS client. It queries the server I specify, or those in resolv.conf, and does not consult etc hosts, mDNS, nscd or systemd-resolved caches. Applications call the C library, which follows the hosts line in nsswitch.conf, typically files first, then DNS, and applies search domains and the ndots setting. So dig can succeed while an application fails because of an entry in etc hosts, a wrong search domain producing a different name, a stub resolver on 127.0.0.53 with a broken upstream, or a negative cache. The right comparison is getent hosts, which uses the same resolution path as the application. With systemd-resolved, resolvectl status shows per-link DNS servers and domains, and resolvectl query shows which source answered. I also test with tcpdump on port 53 to see actual queries, and check for IPv6 AAAA lookups timing out, which produce multi-second delays.
f: What does ndots control?
Why can AAAA lookups cause delays?

q: What is path MTU discovery, and how do you diagnose MTU black holes with ping and tracepath?
p: If a packet is larger than a link's MTU and has the Don't Fragment bit set, the router should return ICMP fragmentation-needed. If ICMP is blocked, large packets silently vanish while small ones work. Test with ping -M do -s and tracepath, and fix with MSS clamping or allowing ICMP.
cmds: ip link show eth0 | grep mtu
sudo iptables -t mangle -A FORWARD -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN -j TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtu
tip: Symptoms: ping and small requests work, but TLS handshakes or large downloads hang. Think MTU first when tunnels or VPNs are involved.
a: Every link has a maximum transmission unit, typically fifteen hundred bytes for Ethernet, less when tunnelling adds headers, as with VPNs, GRE, VXLAN or some cloud overlays. TCP avoids fragmentation using path MTU discovery: it sets the Don't Fragment bit, and a router that cannot forward the packet returns an ICMP fragmentation needed message with the next hop's MTU. If a firewall blocks that ICMP, the sender never learns and large packets disappear, creating a black hole. The signature is that connections establish and small requests work, but anything large, such as a TLS certificate exchange, hangs. I test with ping using the do not fragment flag and varying payload size, and use tracepath to find the MTU along the path. Fixes are to allow ICMP type three code four, lower the MTU on the interface, or clamp TCP MSS on the gateway so endpoints send smaller segments.
f: Why does a VPN reduce MTU?
What does MSS clamping do?

q: How do you read vmstat output to quickly classify a performance problem?
p: vmstat shows the run queue (r), blocked processes (b), swap in and out (si/so), block IO (bi/bo), interrupts, context switches and CPU split (us/sy/id/wa/st). Look at the pattern across lines, not a single snapshot.
tip: r greater than the number of cores means CPU saturation. Non-zero si and so means memory pressure. High wa with b above zero points to storage.
a: I run vmstat with a one second interval for ten or so samples and ignore the first line, which is an average since boot. The r column is the number of runnable processes: consistently higher than the number of CPU cores means CPU saturation. The b column counts processes blocked in uninterruptible sleep, usually waiting for IO. Swap in and swap out values that are non-zero for sustained periods mean real memory pressure. The bi and bo columns show block IO, and wa shows the percentage of time the CPU is idle waiting for IO, so high wa with blocked processes points to storage. High system time with many context switches can mean lock contention or too many threads. The st column shows CPU time stolen by the hypervisor on virtual machines. Once I classify the problem, I drill down with iostat, pidstat, perf or the pressure stall information files.
f: What is pressure stall information?
How do you tell CPU saturation from high utilisation?

q: What are eBPF and the bcc or bpftrace tools, and how do they help production troubleshooting?
p: eBPF runs small verified programs inside the kernel to observe events with low overhead. Tools such as execsnoop, opensnoop, biolatency, tcpconnect and runqlat answer questions that strace or tcpdump can't without heavy cost.
tip: Always say it is safe to run in production because the verifier guarantees programs terminate and cannot crash the kernel.
a: eBPF lets you load small sandboxed programs into the kernel and attach them to events such as system calls, kernel functions, network packets and tracepoints. A verifier checks that they terminate and cannot access invalid memory, so they are safe for production, and the overhead is low because aggregation happens in the kernel. The bcc and bpftrace projects provide ready-made tools. For example, execsnoop shows every new process launched, which finds runaway shell loops, opensnoop shows files being opened, biolatency gives a histogram of disk IO latency, runqlat shows scheduler queueing delay, tcpconnect and tcplife show connection attempts and lifetimes, and profile samples stack traces for CPU flame graphs. I use them when classic tools are not enough or too intrusive, such as finding which process makes a sudden burst of short-lived connections. They require a reasonably recent kernel and root privileges, and the same technology powers Cilium and Falco.
f: Why is strace risky in production?
What does the verifier check?

q: What are Transparent Huge Pages, and why do many database vendors recommend disabling them?
p: THP lets the kernel back memory with 2 MB pages to cut TLB overhead. The background defragmentation and compaction can cause latency spikes and memory bloat for databases with sparse access patterns, so Redis, MongoDB and others advise madvise or never.
tip: Explicit hugepages (hugetlbfs) are different. They are reserved up front, and databases like PostgreSQL can use them deliberately.
a: Normally memory is managed in four kilobyte pages. Using two megabyte huge pages reduces page table size and TLB misses, which can speed up memory-intensive programs. Transparent Huge Pages tries to do this automatically, promoting regions when it can. The downside is that the kernel may have to compact memory to find contiguous blocks, causing stalls, and a khugepaged daemon merges pages in the background. For databases such as Redis, MongoDB and some Java workloads, this produces unpredictable latency spikes and can inflate memory use, for instance copy-on-write of a huge page after fork during a snapshot copies two megabytes for a one byte change. So vendors usually recommend setting it to madvise or never, via the sysfs file and persistently through the boot parameters or a tuned profile. Pre-allocated explicit huge pages remain a good option when I want the benefit with predictable behaviour.
f: THP versus explicit huge pages?
Why does fork plus THP bloat memory?

q: What is NUMA, and how can it cause uneven performance on large servers?
p: On multi-socket machines memory is attached to specific CPUs. Access to remote memory is slower. If a process runs on one node but its memory lives on another, latency rises; unbalanced allocation can exhaust one node while others are free, triggering swapping or OOM.
tip: Mention VMs and containers: pinning a database to a single NUMA node often gives steadier latency than letting threads roam.
a: On servers with more than one CPU socket, each socket has its own memory controller, so memory is split into NUMA nodes. A CPU reaches local memory fast and remote memory over an interconnect with higher latency and lower bandwidth. The kernel tries to allocate local memory, but a large process whose threads run on several nodes, or memory allocated at start by one thread, can end up mostly remote, giving lower and uneven performance. Another problem is imbalance: one node can run out of memory and begin reclaiming or swapping while the machine as a whole shows plenty of free memory. I inspect topology with numactl and lscpu, and per-node usage with numastat. Remedies include pinning processes and memory to a node with numactl or cpuset cgroups, interleaving memory for workloads that need the full capacity, tuning the database's NUMA settings, and, in Kubernetes, using the topology manager with static CPU policy for latency-sensitive pods.
f: What does interleaving do?
How does Kubernetes topology manager help?

q: How do SSH certificates differ from authorized_keys, and why do large fleets use an SSH certificate authority?
p: An SSH CA signs a user's public key with an identity, principals and a short validity. Servers trust the CA key once, so no per-user keys sit in authorized_keys, access expires automatically, and revocation and audit are simpler.
tip: This is the same idea as short-lived cloud credentials: no standing access, a signed token that expires.
a: With plain authorized_keys, every server holds the public keys of everyone allowed, which becomes unmanageable and keys rarely expire, so former staff or lost laptops leave access behind. With an SSH certificate authority, the CA signs a user's public key together with metadata: a key identity for audit, a list of principals, meaning the account names it may log in as, and a validity period such as eight hours. Servers are configured once with the CA's public key using the TrustedUserCAKeys option and optionally principals files. Users get a short-lived certificate after authenticating to an identity system with multi-factor, using tools like Vault, Teleport or Smallstep. When the certificate expires, access ends without any cleanup on servers, and logs show the key identity. Host certificates similarly remove trust-on-first-use warnings. Revoking a lost key is handled by short lifetimes and a revoked keys list.
f: What are principals?
How do host certificates help?

q: firewalld versus ufw versus nftables: how do they relate and how do you choose?
p: nftables is the kernel packet filter that replaced iptables. firewalld and ufw are front ends: firewalld uses zones and runtime versus permanent configuration (RHEL family); ufw is a simple rule syntax (Ubuntu). Use one manager, never mix with hand-edited rules.
cmds: sudo ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/8 to any port 22 proto tcp
tip: In Kubernetes or Docker hosts, remember the container runtime and kube-proxy also write rules, and a firewall manager reload can wipe them.
a: The packet filtering engine in modern kernels is netfilter, now programmed with nftables, which replaced the older iptables interface, though iptables commands often still exist as a compatibility layer. On top of that sit management tools. firewalld, common on the RHEL family, organises interfaces into zones with trust levels and named services, supports runtime and permanent configuration, and can change rules without dropping existing connections. ufw, common on Ubuntu, offers a short, simple syntax for host firewalls. For complex or high-performance rules, such as sets and maps, or for automation in appliances, I may write nftables rules directly. The key is to pick one owner for the rule set. Mixing a manager with manual commands leads to rules being overwritten on reload. On container hosts, Docker and kube-proxy also manage rules, so I check how they interact. In the cloud I combine host firewalls with security groups as defence in depth.
f: What is a firewalld zone?
Why can a firewall reload break Docker networking?

q: What do kernel hardening settings such as kptr_restrict, dmesg_restrict, module signing and lockdown mode protect against?
p: They reduce what a local attacker can learn or load. kptr_restrict hides kernel addresses, dmesg_restrict limits the kernel log, unprivileged_bpf_disabled and ptrace_scope limit tracing and BPF, and module signing or lockdown stops loading unsigned code into the kernel.
tip: Pair these settings with a baseline such as CIS benchmark profiles and verify them with an automated scanner.
a: Many local privilege escalation exploits need information about the kernel layout, or the ability to inspect and manipulate other processes. kptr_restrict hides kernel pointers in files like proc kallsyms from unprivileged users, and dmesg_restrict stops them reading the kernel log, which can leak addresses. The Yama ptrace_scope setting prevents one process from attaching to another unless it is a child, which blocks credential harvesting from running processes. Disabling unprivileged BPF reduces attack surface in the kernel's BPF verifier. On the loading side, kernel module signing, secure boot and lockdown mode prevent root from loading unsigned modules or writing to kernel memory, which defends against rootkits. These are defence in depth, and I apply them through sysctl drop-ins, boot parameters and baseline profiles, validate with a compliance scanner, and test for application impact, as debugging tools like strace or perf may be restricted.
f: What does ptrace_scope protect?
What is secure boot's role?

q: How do LVM snapshots work, and what are the risks of using them for backups?
p: A snapshot is a copy-on-write view of a logical volume at a point in time. Changed blocks are copied into the snapshot space. If that space fills, the snapshot becomes invalid, and write performance on the origin degrades while snapshots exist.
tip: For databases, flush and lock tables or use the database's backup API, because a snapshot is only crash-consistent.
a: When I create an LVM snapshot, LVM reserves some space for it and records the original volume's state. When a block on the origin changes, the old content is first copied into the snapshot area, so the snapshot appears frozen while the origin keeps changing. This is useful for consistent file level backups, rollbacks before risky upgrades, or cloning data for tests. The risks are these. The snapshot space is limited, so if many blocks change and the space fills, the snapshot is invalidated and a backup in progress fails. Every write to the origin triggers an extra copy, so performance drops, sometimes drastically, while the snapshot exists. Snapshots are not backups by themselves, because they live on the same disks. I keep them short-lived, monitor the usage percentage, quiesce applications first, and copy the data off to another system. Thin provisioning improves flexibility.
f: Crash-consistent versus application-consistent?
Why is a snapshot not a backup?

q: What do fstrim and the discard mount option do, and which should you use on SSDs and thin-provisioned storage?
p: TRIM tells the device which blocks are no longer used, helping SSD wear levelling and letting thin-provisioned or cloud storage reclaim space. Continuous discard can hurt performance; a weekly fstrim timer is the usual best practice.
tip: On cloud volumes and VMs, trim support depends on the virtual disk type, so check lsblk --discard shows non-zero granularity.
a: When files are deleted, the filesystem knows blocks are free, but the underlying device does not. TRIM, or discard, informs the device, so an SSD can erase blocks in advance and keep write performance steady, and thin-provisioned storage, such as LVM thin pools, SANs and some virtual disks, can release the space back to the pool. There are two ways to send it. The discard mount option issues commands synchronously as files are deleted, which can add latency and slow deletes on some devices. The alternative is running fstrim periodically, and most distributions ship a systemd timer that does it weekly, which has minimal impact. I prefer the timer. It matters for thin-provisioned virtual machines too, because without it the backing store keeps growing even though the guest shows free space. Encrypted volumes need discard passed through explicitly, with the security trade-off of revealing which blocks are free.
f: Why avoid continuous discard?
How does trim help thin provisioning?

q: On cloud VMs, why do device names like /dev/sdb or nvme1n1 change, and how do you mount disks reliably?
p: Device names depend on probe order and can change across reboots or attachment. NVMe instances present EBS as nvme devices with a different order than the API mapping. Mount by UUID or label, or use stable /dev/disk/by-id paths, and use nofail in fstab for non-critical disks.
tip: A wrong fstab entry without nofail can drop the whole VM into emergency mode at boot, so always run mount -a to test.
a: The kernel assigns names such as sdb or nvme1n1 in the order devices are discovered, which is not guaranteed to stay the same, especially when disks are attached or detached, or when instances use NVMe where the name order does not match the order shown in the cloud console. Mounting by those names in fstab is fragile and can mount the wrong disk. Instead I use the filesystem UUID or a label, which are stored on the disk, or the stable by-id symlinks that include the cloud volume's serial number. I add the nofail option for non-critical data disks, so an absent disk does not stop boot, and use x-systemd.device-timeout to avoid long waits. After editing fstab I always test with mount -a before rebooting. Automation can find the right device using the serial number from lsblk, which maps to the volume ID in the cloud API.
f: Why does nofail matter?
How do you map a volume ID to a device?

q: What is initramfs, what does it do during boot, and how do you rebuild it?
p: The initramfs is a small temporary root filesystem loaded by the bootloader alongside the kernel. It contains drivers and scripts to find and mount the real root filesystem, for example LVM, RAID, LUKS or storage controllers, and then hands over with switch_root.
tip: If the system drops to an initramfs prompt, the root device was not found. Think missing driver, wrong UUID, or a degraded RAID.
a: The kernel cannot mount the real root filesystem unless it has the drivers for the disk controller, filesystem, RAID, LVM or encryption layer, and those might be modules stored on that very filesystem. To solve this chicken and egg problem, the bootloader loads an initial RAM filesystem, a compressed archive that the kernel unpacks into memory and runs. It contains essential modules, udev, and scripts that assemble RAID, unlock LUKS, activate LVM and find root by UUID, then switch to the real root and start init. It's built with dracut on the RHEL family and update-initramfs on Debian-based systems, and must be regenerated after changing storage configuration, drivers, crypttab or when kernels are installed. If boot lands in an initramfs shell, I check for the root device, loaded modules and kernel messages, correct the cause, and rebuild the image from a rescue environment if needed.
f: How do you recover from an initramfs prompt?
What does switch_root do?

q: How do kernel command-line parameters and GRUB configuration work, and how do you change them safely?
p: GRUB reads its configuration and passes a kernel command line, for example root=, ro, quiet, console= and isolcpus. Edit /etc/default/grub then regenerate the config; for a one-off, press e at the GRUB menu to edit the line for a single boot.
tip: Test risky parameters through the temporary edit at the menu first. A mistake there is fixed by rebooting, but a bad permanent change needs a rescue boot.
a: The bootloader, GRUB, loads the kernel and initramfs and passes a string of parameters that configure early boot. Examples are root to locate the root filesystem, ro to mount it read only until fsck, quiet to reduce messages, console to send output to a serial port, which is vital for cloud serial consoles, and tuning options such as isolcpus, hugepages, transparent_hugepage and net.ifnames. The permanent place to set extra options is the GRUB default file, after which I regenerate the configuration file with grub2-mkconfig or update-grub, and on the RHEL family, grubby can modify entries directly. The current values are visible in proc cmdline. When trying something risky, I press e at the boot menu and edit the line for that boot only, so a mistake disappears after reboot. On systems with BLS entries or UEFI, the paths differ, so I check where the real configuration lives before editing.
f: Why set console= on cloud VMs?
What is a BLS entry?

q: What is kdump, and how do you capture and analyse a kernel crash?
p: kdump reserves memory for a second capture kernel that boots after a panic and writes a vmcore of the crashed kernel's memory. You then analyse it with the crash utility and matching kernel debuginfo to see the panic stack and cause.
cmds: echo c | sudo tee /proc/sysrq-trigger   # test only, crashes the host
tip: Never test the sysrq crash on a production host. Use a lab VM.
a: When the kernel panics, the system normally just reboots and the evidence is gone. kdump reserves a region of memory at boot via the crashkernel parameter and preloads a small capture kernel there. On panic, the machine boots into that capture kernel, which saves the crashed kernel's memory image as a vmcore to disk, network or another target, then reboots. To analyse it, I use the crash tool along with the debuginfo for the exact kernel version, and commands like bt for the backtrace, log for the kernel messages and ps to see processes at the time. This identifies a faulty driver, a hung task or memory corruption, and gives vendors the data to analyse. It must be configured and tested ahead of time, with enough reserved memory and disk space, and sometimes watchdog and panic-on-oops settings so hung machines actually trigger a dump.
f: What does the crashkernel parameter do?
Why do you need matching debuginfo?

q: How do /etc/security/limits.conf and systemd resource settings interact for users and services?
p: limits.conf is applied by pam_limits for login sessions. Services started by systemd ignore it and use LimitNOFILE, LimitNPROC, TasksMax and similar directives in unit files or drop-ins, with defaults in system.conf. Check the live values in /proc/<pid>/limits.
cmds: sudo systemctl edit myapp   # add [Service] LimitNOFILE=65536
tip: Always verify against the running process, because what the file says and what the process got can differ.
a: Resource limits are set per process, inherited from the parent. For interactive logins, the PAM module pam_limits reads etc security limits.conf and the limits.d directory and applies soft and hard limits per user or group, such as open files, processes, core size and locked memory. A service started by systemd never goes through a PAM login session, so those files do not affect it. Instead, I set directives such as LimitNOFILE, LimitNPROC, LimitCORE or LimitMEMLOCK in the unit file, preferably through a drop-in created with systemctl edit, followed by a daemon reload and restart. There is also TasksMax controlling the number of tasks in the unit's cgroup, which limits threads and processes. Global defaults can be changed in system.conf. To check what applies, I read the limits file for the running process under proc, which is the source of truth, and not the config files.
f: What is TasksMax?
How do soft and hard limits differ?

q: How should you set up service accounts on Linux: system users, nologin shells, and running services without root?
p: Create a system user with no login shell and no home unless needed, run the service under it with systemd User= and hardening options, bind low ports via capabilities or a proxy, and keep files owned by that user with minimal permissions.
cmds: sudo systemctl edit app   # User=appsvc, NoNewPrivileges=yes, ProtectSystem=strict
tip: systemd-analyze security gives a score and shows which sandboxing options you are still missing.
a: A service should never run as root unless there is a genuine need. I create a dedicated system account using the system flag, so it gets a low UID in the reserved range, no password, no home directory unless the app needs one, and a nologin shell so nobody can log in as it. In the unit file I set the user and group, and use systemd sandboxing options such as NoNewPrivileges, ProtectSystem, ProtectHome, PrivateTmp, and restricting capabilities and address families. If the program has to listen on a port below one thousand twenty-four, I grant just the net bind service capability, use socket activation, or put a reverse proxy in front. File ownership and permissions are restricted to the service account, with secrets readable only by it. Systemd-analyze security audits the unit and highlights what remains exposed. Each service gets its own account, so compromise of one does not give access to others.
f: What does NoNewPrivileges do?
Why one account per service?

q: How do you parse command-line options in a bash script, and when should you switch to a more capable language?
p: Use getopts for short options in portable scripts, or a while-case loop for long options. Validate arguments, print usage on error and exit non-zero. When option handling, data structures or error handling become complex, move to Python or Go.
cmds: while getopts ':e:vh' opt; do case $opt in e) env=$OPTARG;; v) verbose=1;; h) usage; exit 0;; \?) usage; exit 2;; esac; done; shift $((OPTIND-1))
tip: Send errors to stderr and use distinct exit codes, so automation can tell usage mistakes from runtime failures.
a: For simple scripts I use the getopts builtin. I define the allowed short options in a string, loop over them in a case statement, handle unknown options and missing arguments explicitly, and shift away the processed options so the remaining positional parameters are available. For long options such as dash dash environment, I write a while loop with case matching on the argument and shift. I always validate required values, quote all variables, print a usage message to standard error on misuse and exit with a non-zero code, using two for usage errors and one for runtime failures. As soon as a script needs nested data structures, JSON handling, retries, concurrency, richer error handling or tests, I switch to Python or Go, where argparse or cobra gives better help text and validation. A good rule is that if the bash script passes about a hundred lines or needs arrays of arrays, rewrite it.
f: What does shift do?
Why exit codes matter for automation?

q: How do you use trap and flock in bash to clean up after failures and prevent concurrent runs?
p: trap runs a handler on EXIT, ERR or signals, so temp files are removed and locks released even on failure. flock takes an advisory lock on a file descriptor, so a second instance exits or waits instead of running concurrently, and the lock is released automatically if the process dies.
tip: Prefer flock over a hand-made pid file, since a crashed script leaves a stale pid file but cannot leave a stale flock.
a: Robust scripts clean up after themselves. The trap builtin registers a command to run when a signal arrives or on pseudo-signals such as EXIT, which fires however the script ends, and ERR, which fires when a command fails. A common pattern is to create a temporary directory with mktemp and trap EXIT to remove it, so interrupted runs do not leak files. To stop two copies of a job, such as a backup scheduled by cron, overlapping, I use flock. I open a lock file on a file descriptor and call flock with the non-blocking option, exiting if it cannot take the lock. Because the kernel releases the lock when the process exits, even by crashing, there are no stale lock problems like with pid files. In cron I can also wrap the command with flock directly. Together with set minus euo pipefail, this makes scripts safe to re-run.
f: Why is a pid file unreliable?
What does the ERR trap not catch?

q: How do you use jq (and yq) in shell pipelines to work safely with JSON and YAML?
p: jq filters and transforms JSON with a small expression language. Use -r for raw strings, --arg to pass shell values safely, select to filter, map for arrays, and exit-status flags to fail the script on missing data. yq does the same for YAML.
cmds: kubectl get pods -o json | jq -r --arg ns prod '.items[] | select(.metadata.namespace==$ns) | .metadata.name'
tip: Never build jq filters by string-concatenating user input. Pass values with --arg so quoting cannot break or inject.
a: Parsing JSON with grep and sed is fragile, so I use jq. A filter starts from the input with dot, navigates fields, iterates arrays with brackets, and can pipe results to further filters. Select keeps items that match a condition, map transforms arrays, and output formats like at tsv and at csv produce shell-friendly rows. The raw output flag removes JSON quotes from strings, which matters when assigning to shell variables. When I need a shell value inside the filter, I pass it with the arg option rather than interpolating it into the program text, which avoids quoting bugs and injection. The exit-status flag makes jq return a non-zero code when the result is false or null, so scripts can fail fast on unexpected data. yq provides a similar syntax for YAML, handy for Kubernetes manifests and CI configuration, and I check which yq implementation is installed because there are two with different syntax.
f: Why pass values with --arg?
What does jq -e do?

q: Load average is very high but CPU utilisation is low. What is happening and how do you find the cause?
p: Linux load average counts runnable tasks and tasks in uninterruptible sleep (D state), usually waiting on IO. High load with idle CPU points to blocked IO such as slow disks or hung NFS. Find D-state processes and what they wait on.
tip: The wchan column tells you which kernel function the process is blocked in, a quick clue for NFS, disk or lock waits.
a: On Linux, load average includes not just tasks that are running or ready to run, but also those in uninterruptible sleep, state D, which are normally waiting for IO to complete. So a machine whose processes are blocked on a slow or hung disk, a stuck NFS mount, a failing storage path or a lock can show a load of fifty while the CPU sits idle. I confirm by looking at vmstat for the blocked column and high wait percentage, then list processes in D state and the kernel function they wait in using wchan or proc stack. Iostat shows device latency and utilisation, and mount output reveals network filesystems. Typical causes are NFS server outages with hard mounts, a failing disk, an overloaded cloud volume that exhausted burst credits, or a backup job saturating IO. The fix is to restore the storage path, throttle the offender with ionice, or use soft mount options where appropriate.
f: Why can't you kill a D-state process?
Why do hard NFS mounts hang clients?

q: Disk latency spikes on a cloud VM every few hours even though the workload is steady. What do you check?
p: Look for exhausted burst credits or throttling on the volume or instance, snapshots or backups running, filesystem maintenance, and noisy neighbours. Compare iostat await with the cloud provider's volume metrics.
cmds: aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name BurstBalance --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-1 ...
tip: gp2 burst balance and instance-level EBS bandwidth limits are two separate throttles. Check both.
a: I first confirm the problem in the guest with iostat: high await and queue size with utilisation near one hundred percent shows the device is saturated or throttled. A periodic pattern suggests a scheduled cause or a credit cycle. In clouds, volumes may have burst credits, like older gp2 volumes or small burstable disks, so the workload runs fast until credits are exhausted, then drops to the baseline until they refill. The instance also has its own storage bandwidth and IOPS limits, which can be hit even if the volume has capacity. I check the provider's metrics for burst balance, throttling and queue length. Locally I look for cron jobs, log rotation, backups, snapshots, database checkpoints or fstrim running at those times using iotop. Fixes include moving to a volume type with provisioned performance, increasing volume size, choosing a larger instance, spreading scheduled jobs, and using ionice for background tasks.
f: How do gp3 and gp2 differ for bursting?
What does await measure?

q: Services fail with 'Too many open files' under load, but ulimit -n in your shell shows a high value. Why?
p: The service process has a different limit from your shell: it inherited the systemd default or its own LimitNOFILE. Check /proc/<pid>/limits for the real values, then set LimitNOFILE in the unit and look for a descriptor leak.
cmds: lsof -p $(pidof myapp) | awk '{print $5}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr
tip: Also check fs.file-max and the container runtime's own limits when the service runs inside Docker or Kubernetes.
a: Limits belong to each process, so what my interactive shell shows is irrelevant to a daemon that started earlier under systemd with its own settings. I read the running process's limits file to see the true soft and hard values, and compare with how many descriptors it has open, counted from its fd directory. If the count approaches the limit, I check whether this is legitimate growth or a leak. Using lsof and grouping by type shows whether the descriptors are sockets in CLOSE_WAIT, deleted files, or pipes, which points at the code not closing resources. As an immediate fix I raise LimitNOFILE with a systemd drop-in and restart, and for containers I check the runtime default and the node level maximums. If a leak is confirmed, raising limits only delays the failure, so I fix the code, add connection timeouts and pooling, and monitor the open descriptor count as a metric.
f: Why does raising the limit not fix a leak?
How would you alert on descriptor usage?

q: SSH logins are slow, with a long pause before the password or key prompt. What are the usual causes?
p: The server does a reverse DNS lookup of the client (UseDNS), GSSAPI authentication tries Kerberos and times out, or the login path is slow due to PAM, SSSD or a hung home directory mount. Use ssh -vvv and server logs to find the stall.
tip: Timing the verbose client output shows exactly where the delay happens: before key exchange, before auth, or after login.
a: I run the client with triple verbose and watch where the output pauses. A delay before the key exchange or banner often comes from the server doing a reverse DNS lookup on the client's address, controlled by UseDNS, when the resolver is slow or unreachable. A pause during authentication method negotiation commonly comes from GSSAPI trying Kerberos with an unreachable KDC, so disabling GSSAPIAuthentication for clients that do not need it fixes it. If the delay occurs after authentication succeeds, the cause is on the server side in PAM modules, an SSSD or LDAP lookup that is slow, systemd-logind taking time to create the session, or a home directory on a slow or hung NFS mount. I check the sshd logs and the time getent takes for user lookups. The fix is correcting DNS settings, disabling unneeded features, and repairing the identity backend.
f: What does UseDNS do?
How can SSSD cause slow logins?

q: TLS errors, Kerberos failures or odd log timestamps appear on some servers. How could clock drift be the cause, and how do you fix it?
p: Certificates have validity windows and Kerberos tolerates only minutes of skew. If NTP is down or the clock steps, validation fails. Check chronyc tracking, sync sources and virtualisation time sync, then step the clock safely and fix the time source.
tip: On VMs, avoid two competing time sync mechanisms such as the hypervisor tools and chrony both adjusting the clock.
a: Many security protocols depend on accurate time. TLS clients reject certificates that are not yet valid or already expired by the local clock, Kerberos allows only a few minutes of skew between client, server and KDC, and distributed systems such as databases and tokens rely on clocks for ordering and expiry. If a server drifts, I see certificate not yet valid errors, authentication failures, or logs that do not line up between hosts. I check timedatectl for synchronisation state, and chronyc tracking for the current offset and sources. Causes include NTP blocked by a firewall, a bad or unreachable time source, a paused VM or live migration, or conflicting sync mechanisms. I fix connectivity, point to reliable internal sources, and let chrony slew gently, using makestep for a large initial correction, being careful that stepping the clock can disrupt applications. Monitoring offset across the fleet catches drift early.
f: Slewing versus stepping the clock?
Why use internal NTP servers?

q: A log file is not rotating and the disk is filling. How do you diagnose logrotate problems?
p: Test the config with logrotate -d, check the state file and timer or cron, permissions and SELinux, and whether the app keeps writing to the old inode. Use copytruncate or a postrotate signal so the app reopens its log.
tip: After rotation the app must reopen its file, otherwise it keeps writing to the renamed file or a deleted inode and space is not freed.
a: I begin with a debug dry run of the specific config, which shows whether logrotate considers the file, why it skips it, and any syntax or permission errors. Then I check that logrotate is actually being triggered by its systemd timer or cron job, and the state file for the last rotation time. Common problems are a glob pattern that does not match, wrong ownership or permissions on the directory so logrotate refuses to rotate, SELinux denials, a size or time condition not yet met, or a failing postrotate script that aborts. Even when rotation works, space might not be freed if the application holds the old file open and continues writing to the renamed or deleted file. The fix is a postrotate command that signals the app to reopen logs, or copytruncate for apps that cannot, accepting a small risk of losing lines. I also add compression, a retention count and monitoring on disk usage.
f: copytruncate trade-offs?
Why isn't space freed after rotation?

q: The system is swapping heavily and everything is slow, but free shows a lot of memory used by cache. What is going on?
p: Page cache is reclaimable and counted in available memory. Heavy swapping suggests real anonymous memory pressure, a swappiness setting that favours swapping, memory cgroup limits, or a leak. Check available, si/so, and per-process swap usage.
cmds: for f in /proc/*/status; do awk '/Name|VmSwap/{printf $2" "} END{print ""}' $f; done | sort -k2 -nr | head
tip: Read the available column, not free. Cache will be dropped when needed, but anonymous memory has to be swapped.
a: I start by reading the available column from free, which estimates memory that can be given to applications without swapping, because cache and buffers can be reclaimed. If available is low, there is real pressure from anonymous memory such as heaps. Vmstat shows ongoing swap in and swap out activity, and sustained non-zero values mean the system is thrashing. I identify the biggest swap users by looking at VmSwap per process, and check whether one process is leaking, whether a memory cgroup limit forces its processes into swap, or whether many processes simply need more RAM than the host has. Swappiness influences how eagerly the kernel swaps versus dropping cache, but it is not the root cause. Remedies are fixing the leak, reducing workload, adding memory, tuning limits, and for databases lowering swappiness. If the system is unusable, I may need to restart the offending service, and use pressure stall information to monitor.
f: What does swappiness control?
What is memory pressure stall information?

q: A client sees 'connection refused' sometimes, 'timed out' other times, and 'reset by peer' on others. What does each tell you?
p: Refused means a host answered with RST because nothing is listening or a firewall rejects. Timed out means packets were dropped silently, or the path or host is down. Reset by peer means the connection was established and then forcibly closed by the peer, a proxy, or a firewall idle timeout.
cmds: sudo tcpdump -ni any host 10.0.0.5 and port 443
tip: Capture packets at both ends if you can. Seeing who sends the RST or where the SYN stops settles most arguments.
a: Each message points at a different layer. Connection refused is quick: the destination host is reachable and its kernel replied with a reset because no process is listening on that port, or a firewall rule explicitly rejects. I check that the service is running, listening on the right address, and the rules. Timed out means no reply at all, so packets are being dropped, from a firewall with a drop rule, a security group, a routing problem, an unreachable host, or an overloaded listen queue. I trace the path and capture packets to see whether SYNs arrive. Connection reset by peer happens after the connection exists, when the other side, or a device in the middle like a load balancer, NAT or firewall, sends a reset, for instance after an idle timeout, an application crash or a protocol error. Packet captures show who sent the reset and when, which tells me where to look next.
f: Why would a firewall send RST instead of dropping?
How do idle timeouts cause resets?

q: Latency is bad and ethtool shows RX drops or the listen queue overflows. How do you tell NIC, kernel and application limits apart?
p: Check NIC counters (rx_dropped, rx_missed), softirq CPU usage, ring buffer sizes, the accept queue (ss, nstat ListenOverflows), and backlog sysctls. Tune ring buffers, RSS/IRQ affinity, somaxconn and the app's backlog, or scale out.
tip: A single CPU at 100 percent softirq while others idle usually means interrupts are not spread across cores.
a: I look at three places. First, NIC level counters from ethtool: rx dropped or missed counts rising mean the card or its ring buffer overflowed because the kernel did not drain packets fast enough, which I can ease by increasing ring sizes or spreading interrupts across CPUs with receive side scaling and IRQ affinity. Second, the kernel network stack: softnet statistics showing drops or time squeeze, and one core saturated in softirq. Third, the application's accept queue: listen overflow and drop counters in nstat, together with the Recv-Q of a listening socket from ss, show that the app does not accept connections fast enough or its backlog is capped by somaxconn. Fixes depend on the layer: tune ring buffers and interrupt distribution, raise somaxconn and the application backlog, add worker threads or processes, or scale horizontally behind a load balancer. I validate under load with before and after counters.
f: What is RSS in networking?
What does time squeeze mean in softnet_stat?

q: A filesystem suddenly became read-only on a running server. What happened and how do you recover?
p: ext4 and XFS remount read-only on errors by default (errors=remount-ro) to protect data. Causes include disk or controller errors, cloud volume detach, or corruption. Check dmesg, stop writers, run fsck from a rescue or after unmount, and replace failing hardware.
tip: On cloud VMs, a brief volume detach or storage incident often causes this, so check provider events before assuming corruption.
a: When the kernel detects metadata errors or IO failures, filesystems like ext4 by default remount themselves read-only to avoid making damage worse, which shows up as applications failing to write. I check dmesg for the first error, which usually points to the cause: hardware IO errors, a SCSI or NVMe timeout, a storage path failure, or corruption after an unclean shutdown. In the cloud I check whether the volume had an incident, was resized, or briefly lost connectivity. Recovery starts by stopping the applications, taking a backup or snapshot of the volume if possible, then unmounting the filesystem, or booting into a rescue environment for the root volume, and running fsck, or xfs_repair for XFS, to repair it, before remounting read-write. If errors recur, the underlying disk is unhealthy, so I check SMART data, replace it and restore from backup. Monitoring for ro mounts and IO errors gives early warning.
f: What does errors=remount-ro do?
Why shouldn't you fsck a mounted filesystem?

q: A file has mode 777 and you are root, yet you get 'Permission denied' executing or writing it. What else can block access?
p: Check mount options (noexec, ro, nosuid), SELinux or AppArmor denials, immutable attributes, missing execute permission on a parent directory, a bad interpreter line (CRLF), ACL masks, and filesystem type limits such as FAT or NFS root squash.
cmds: ls -lZ /opt/app/run.sh; getenforce; sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent
tip: Work down a checklist rather than guessing: mount, MAC, attributes, ACL, path, interpreter.
a: Standard permission bits are only one layer. If execution fails, the filesystem may be mounted noexec, which is common on tmp directories, or read-only for writes, and findmnt shows the mount options. Mandatory access control systems like SELinux or AppArmor can deny the operation even for root, and the audit log or journal shows an AVC denial with the context involved. File attributes such as immutable block modification, ACL entries and the ACL mask can restrict effective permissions beyond the mode, and every directory in the path needs the execute bit for traversal. For scripts, a bad shebang line caused by Windows line endings or a missing interpreter produces a misleading no such file or permission error. On network filesystems, root squash maps root to an unprivileged user. I work through this checklist systematically, find the layer that denies access, and fix it correctly rather than loosening permissions broadly.
f: What is root squash?
How do you read an AVC denial?

q: A systemd service fails to start with status=203/EXEC or 'Failed at step USER'. How do you diagnose it?
p: 203/EXEC means systemd could not execute the binary: wrong path, no execute bit, missing interpreter, noexec mount or SELinux label. Failed at step USER means the configured user does not exist. Read systemctl status and journalctl -u, then test the command as that user.
tip: systemctl cat shows the effective unit including drop-ins, which is where surprise overrides hide.
a: The status output includes the main process exit status, and the service journal gives more detail. Status 203 EXEC means systemd failed to execute the command in ExecStart, so I check that the path is absolute and exists, the file has the execute bit, the interpreter named in the shebang exists, the filesystem is not mounted noexec, and SELinux allows execution of that label. Messages like failed at step USER or GROUP mean the account named in the unit does not exist or cannot be resolved. Other step names help too: CHDIR for a missing working directory, NAMESPACE for sandboxing options that cannot be applied, and CAPABILITIES for capability issues. I run the command by hand as the same user and environment to reproduce, review the effective unit with systemctl cat to catch drop-in overrides, validate with systemd-analyze verify, then reload the daemon and restart. Setting Restart and rate limits avoids tight failure loops.
f: What does 'failed at step NAMESPACE' mean?
How do drop-ins override units?

q: A cron job runs fine by hand but never runs or fails silently from cron. How do you debug it?
p: Cron runs with a minimal environment (PATH, no profile), a different working directory and no TTY. Check syslog or journal for CRON entries, mail output, the crontab syntax and user, absolute paths, permissions, and redirect output to a log.
cmds: grep CRON /var/log/syslog | tail   # or journalctl -u cron
tip: Dumping env from a test cron entry shows precisely how different the cron environment is from your shell.
a: Cron starts commands with a very small environment: a minimal PATH, no profile files, a home directory as the working directory, and no terminal, so scripts relying on aliases, environment variables or relative paths break. My first step is checking that the job is being triggered at all, by looking for CRON entries in syslog or the journal, which also reveals syntax errors and wrong user fields in files under etc cron.d, where a user column is required unlike in a user crontab. If it is triggered but fails, I redirect standard output and error to a log file, since by default cron tries to mail output. I use absolute paths for all commands, set PATH and needed variables at the top of the crontab or script, make the script executable with a proper shebang, and check percent signs, which cron treats specially. A flock wrapper prevents overlapping runs, and systemd timers are an alternative with better logging.
f: Why are percent signs a problem in crontab?
Cron versus systemd timers?

q: Processes are stuck in D state after an NFS server outage, and the client hangs on ls or df. How do you recover?
p: Hard NFS mounts block forever waiting for the server by design. Restore the server or network, or use umount -f / -l and, if mounted with intr or soft options, interrupt. As a last resort, reboot. Prevent with soft,timeo options where safe, autofs and monitoring.
tip: Never run df or ls on a suspected hung NFS mount without timeout, or your own shell joins the D-state pile.
a: By default NFS uses hard mounts, so if the server disappears the client keeps retrying forever, and processes touching that mount sleep in uninterruptible state, which cannot be killed, and even df or ls can hang. The best recovery is to restore the server or the network path, after which the processes continue. If that cannot happen soon, I try a forced and lazy unmount, which detaches the mount point from the namespace so new accesses do not hang, though processes already blocked may stay stuck until the server returns or the host reboots. To find affected mounts safely I use commands wrapped in timeout. For prevention I design for failure: use soft mounts only for data where errors are acceptable, because they can corrupt writes, tune timeo and retrans, use autofs to mount on demand, avoid critical paths depending on NFS, monitor server health, and use NFS version four with a highly available server.
f: Soft versus hard NFS mounts?
What does lazy unmount do?

q: A database server shows irregular latency spikes. How would you check transparent huge pages, swap, NUMA and IO scheduler settings together?
p: Review each known source of stalls in order: THP and compaction, swap activity, NUMA imbalance, dirty page writeback bursts, IO scheduler and queue depth, and CPU frequency or C-states. Correlate spikes with kernel counters rather than guessing.
tip: Capture counters before and after a spike, so you compare numbers instead of opinions.
a: I treat it as a checklist of known stall sources and measure each during a spike. For memory, I read the compaction and THP counters in vmstat, because direct compaction and huge page splitting can pause allocations, and check that transparent huge pages are set to madvise or never for the database. I check swap activity and the swappiness setting. For NUMA, I look at per-node memory with numastat, since one node running low can force reclaim while others are free. Writeback matters: large dirty page ratios allow big bursts of flushing that block writers, so I lower dirty background ratios so flushing is steadier. For storage I check the IO scheduler, such as none or mq-deadline for NVMe, the queue depth, and device latency in iostat. Finally, CPU frequency scaling and deep C-states can add wake-up latency. I change one thing at a time and measure.
f: Why lower dirty ratios for databases?
Which IO scheduler suits NVMe?

q: You find an unexpected listening port on a production server. How do you identify what owns it and decide whether it is malicious?
p: Map the port to a process with ss -tlnp or lsof, then examine the binary path, hash, parent, start time, package ownership, systemd unit and network connections. Compare to a baseline, isolate if suspicious, and preserve evidence before killing.
tip: A binary running from /tmp, a deleted executable (exe -> (deleted)) or no package owner are strong red flags.
a: First I map the listener to a process with ss or lsof, which gives the process ID, user and command. Then I look at the evidence under proc: the executable path, command line, current working directory, environment and open files, and when it started. I check whether the binary belongs to an installed package with the package manager and verify its hash against the package or a known good source. Strong warning signs are execution from temp directories, a deleted binary that is still running, an unusual parent process, a name imitating a system process, or outbound connections to unfamiliar addresses. I compare against a baseline or configuration management inventory to see if the service is expected. If it looks malicious I isolate the host from the network rather than just killing the process, capture memory and process information, preserve logs, and follow the incident response process before cleaning up. If it is legitimate, I document and firewall it appropriately.
f: Why isolate before killing?
How do you verify a binary against its package?

q: The disk under /var/lib/docker is full on a container host. What do you clean up safely, and how do you stop it recurring?
p: Find what consumes space with docker system df: unused images, stopped containers, build cache, volumes and oversized container logs. Prune carefully, set log rotation limits, put Docker data on its own volume, and alert on usage.
tip: Container JSON logs without max-size are the most common silent disk eater. Set log-opts in daemon.json.
a: I start with docker system df to see how space is divided between images, containers, local volumes and build cache, and use du on the containers directory to spot giant JSON log files. Safe cleanups are removing stopped containers, dangling and unused images older than a week or so, and old build cache. I am careful with volumes, since they may hold real data, and never prune them blindly. A runaway log file can be truncated if the container must keep running. To prevent recurrence I configure the logging driver defaults in daemon.json with max-size and max-file, or use a driver that ships logs elsewhere, put Docker's data root on a dedicated volume so it cannot fill the root filesystem, schedule regular pruning in CI runners, use smaller base images and multi-stage builds, set ephemeral-storage requests and limits in Kubernetes, and alert at eighty percent usage.
f: Why not prune volumes blindly?
How do you set log limits in daemon.json?

q: A Java or Go service in a container gets OOMKilled, but the heap looks fine. Which non-heap memory and cgroup details do you check?
p: The cgroup limit covers heap plus metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers, mmap'd files, native libraries and page cache attributed to the cgroup. Compare memory.current and memory.stat with runtime metrics and leave headroom.
tip: Rule of thumb: set JVM heap to roughly 60 to 75 percent of the container limit, not 100 percent.
a: The kernel enforces the cgroup memory limit on everything the container uses, not just the language heap. For a JVM that includes metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, direct and mapped buffers, GC structures and native libraries, and the page cache for files the container reads and writes also counts, though it can be reclaimed. A Go program has stacks, runtime overhead and memory not yet returned to the operating system. I read the cgroup's current usage and its stat file to see the split between anonymous memory, file cache, kernel memory and sockets, and compare it with runtime metrics such as native memory tracking. Then I adjust: size the heap as a percentage of the container limit, limit thread counts and direct memory, set GOMEMLIMIT for Go, and raise the limit if the process legitimately needs it. I also check dmesg for the kill details and whether a sidecar, rather than the app, was the victim.
f: What is GOMEMLIMIT?
Does page cache count toward the limit?

q: What do umask and the setgid directory bit do together to create a secure shared project directory?
p: umask removes permission bits from newly created files. The setgid bit on a directory makes new files inherit the directory's group. Together, with a project group and umask 002 or default ACLs, team members can collaborate without opening files to everyone.
cmds: sudo groupadd proj && sudo mkdir /srv/proj && sudo chgrp proj /srv/proj
tip: Default ACLs are more reliable than relying on every user's umask, because they apply regardless of how the file was created.
a: For a shared directory I create a dedicated group, make it the directory's group, and set mode two seven seven zero. The leading two is the setgid bit, so every file and subdirectory created inside inherits the project group instead of the creator's primary group, and the zero for others keeps outsiders out. The remaining problem is that new files are created according to the creator's umask, and with the common umask of zero two two, group members cannot write files made by someone else. I can set umask zero zero two for the team, but that depends on each user's shell setup. A more robust approach is a default ACL on the directory granting the group read, write and execute, which new files inherit regardless of umask. Removing others entirely and adding the sticky bit where users should not delete each other's files completes the design.
f: What does the sticky bit do?

q: What are sparse files, and how can they make du, ls and df disagree?
p: A sparse file has holes: ranges never written that take no disk blocks but read back as zeros. ls shows the apparent size, du shows blocks actually allocated, and a full-looking VM image can use far less space. Copying without sparse support can balloon it.
cmds: truncate -s 10G disk.img; ls -lh disk.img; du -h disk.img
tip: This explains why a database or VM image can fill a disk later than its apparent size suggests.
a: A sparse file is one where regions that were never written are not backed by disk blocks. When you read them you get zeros, but they consume no space. You can create one with truncate to extend the file size, or by seeking past the end before writing. This is why ls minus l, which reports the apparent length, can show ten gigabytes while du, which counts allocated blocks, shows almost nothing. Virtual machine images, some database files and core dumps are often sparse. The surprises come later. A naive copy or backup tool that reads the zeros and writes them out turns a small file into a full-sized one, so I use sparse-aware options in cp, rsync or tar. Also, a sparse file can fill the disk unexpectedly as it is written, because the filesystem promised more logical space than physical space it has, which is thin provisioning inside a file. Fallocate preallocates real blocks when I need guarantees.
f: How does fallocate differ from truncate?
How do you copy a sparse file efficiently?

q: How do you use pidstat, top -H and /proc to find which thread of a multi-threaded process is hot?
p: Per-thread views show what a per-process view hides. top -H and pidstat -t list threads with their CPU use; the thread ID can be converted to hex to match a Java thread dump, or used with perf and gdb to see its stack.
tip: The Java trick, converting the hot thread's TID to hex and finding nid in the thread dump, is a classic interview demonstration.
a: A process that appears to use one hundred fifty percent CPU may have one runaway thread or many moderately busy threads, and the fix is different. top with the H option shows individual threads, and pidstat with the t flag reports CPU use per thread over time. Once I have the busiest thread ID, I can look at proc for its name and state, and use perf top or perf record on that task ID to see where it spends time. For a Java application, I convert the thread ID to hexadecimal, take a thread dump with jstack, and search for the matching native ID, which shows the exact stack trace of the hot thread, perhaps a GC thread, a spin loop or a regex. For Go, pprof profiles goroutines, and for Python, py-spy attaches without restarting. This workflow narrows the problem from machine to process to thread to code line.
f: How do you profile a Go service?
What does py-spy do?

q: Why should shell scripts quote variables and avoid parsing ls, and what are safe patterns for looping over files?
p: Unquoted variables undergo word splitting and globbing, so filenames with spaces or asterisks break or expand unexpectedly. ls output is not reliably parseable. Use globs, find -print0 with xargs -0 or while read -r -d '', and quote everything.
cmds: for f in ./*.log; do [ -e "$f" ] || continue; gzip -- "$f"; done
while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do echo "$f"; done < <(find . -type f -print0)
tip: Run shellcheck in CI. It catches most quoting bugs before they reach production.
a: In bash, an unquoted variable is split on whitespace and then subject to filename expansion, so a file named my report dot txt becomes two arguments, and a variable containing an asterisk expands to every file in the directory. That has deleted real data in production scripts, for example with rm of a path built from an empty variable. So I quote every expansion and use double dash to end option parsing for names that may start with a hyphen. Parsing ls output is wrong because filenames can contain spaces, newlines and other special characters. Safe patterns are looping over a glob directly, checking the file exists to handle no matches, or using find with print0 so names are separated by null bytes, consumed by xargs minus zero or a while read loop with the null delimiter. I also use set minus u to catch unset variables, and run shellcheck as part of CI.
f: Why does an empty variable make rm dangerous?
What does set -u do?
